name: Nikhil Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I work with the independent Work Futures Panel. We are not linked to your insurer, AI companies or government, and this stays confidential. Tell me about a normal day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I supervise the policy paperwork desk at an insurer. I graduated with a bachelor's degree, but the useful education came from spotting where a renewal form contradicts the old policy. I assign the inbox, clear hard cases and take my lunch at the same little table by the window.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being the person a newer clerk can ask without feeling foolish. I dislike another new screen for something we can already do, and I have never used an AI tool myself. A careful clerk should be able to put a name to the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the desk to carry on checking renewals properly. If AI just speeds up filing, we can use the time to clear the old policy corrections.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have a few months of expenses saved, and my pay covers my small rented place. Still, the insurer has left one vacancy open since spring, so even a small time saving might become an excuse not to replace anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep my paper checklist beside the renewal queue and ask the manager whether the empty desk will be filled. I'll put a little from each paycheque aside before buying anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly because of the vacancy, not because I expect to lose my own place tomorrow. I know the desk works better with enough people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the vacant desk mean to your team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The junior clerks lose a teacher if that empty desk becomes the normal staffing plan. I would tell the manager our correction pile has grown, even while the daily count looks fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much could you actually save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can save perhaps seventy a month while rent stays fixed. My savings might carry me through a short search, but there are only some other insurance desks nearby.

say: I'd tell colleagues to **check renewals** properly and use any spare time on corrections.
I'd point out the **open vacancy** and ask whether it will be filled.
think: I fear mild automation may become a reason to **leave a desk empty**.
My modest savings would fund only a **short local search**.
do: Keep the **paper checklist** beside the renewal queue.
Ask the manager this month whether the **vacant desk** will be filled.
Save about **seventy monthly** while rent remains fixed.
feel: **Uneasy** about staffing, though his own job seems safe for now.
S0.quote: I know the desk works better with enough people.
fieldNote: He values **named responsibility** and sees a vacant post as a warning.
His **few months of savings** are a bridge, not secure retirement money.
He still uses a **paper checklist** and has never tried AI himself.

steps.text: Keep checking renewal forms with his paper checklist
Ask manager this month whether the vacant policy desk will be filled
Save seventy from each monthly paycheque while rent remains fixed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should not promise customers a quick renewal if nobody checks the exclusions. Writing and checking are most of our work; software taking those tasks would hit this desk early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the insurer might cut my hours or merge my team into another office. I am good at the difficult forms, but a manager could decide one clerk checks what four clerks used to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring a month of correction records to the manager and ask for a staffing meeting. If paid hours fall in the first year, I'd trim restaurant meals and search the other insurers nearby before giving notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I do not like the idea of bargaining for my own hours, but rent comes every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask in the staffing meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not tell the team every job is safe. I would ask the manager which policy checks still require a named employee and when the next staffing decision is due.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the new system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might learn the approved system if it is required for my current role, after someone shows me the mistakes it makes. I would not pay for a course on my own just because a brochure says there will be jobs.

say: I'd say **policy exclusions** need checking before customers receive quick promises.
I'd ask management which checks require a **named employee**.
think: My **hours may shrink** if one clerk supervises several software streams.
I would learn a required tool only after seeing its **mistakes**.
do: Bring **one month of corrections** to a staffing meeting.
Cut **restaurant meals** if my paid hours fall.
Search **nearby insurers** only if my paid hours fall, before leaving this job.
feel: **Anxious** because his own hours could realistically shrink.
S1.quote: Writing and checking are most of our work; software taking those tasks would hit this desk early.
fieldNote: He identifies **writing and checking** as the desk's immediate exposure.
He would accept a **required approved tool** with evidence and instruction.
His search starts after **paid hours fall** and before he gives notice.

steps.text: Bring one month of policy corrections to insurer staffing meeting
Cut restaurant meals if paid insurance hours fall
Contact nearby insurers only if paid hours fall, before leaving current job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my colleagues AGI by 2028 is the sharpest threat to policy paperwork. It could reason through exclusions and renewals by then; robots around 2031 do not give our desk extra time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the insurer to cut most of our team, including my own post, if full thinking AI is cheaper. I have been waking at night thinking about the rent and the people I supervise, though I know the card is only a picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd ask for a written account of redundancy terms and keep my current wages while the job exists. If my post goes in 2028, I'd apply for paid claims and policy roles only where a vacancy is advertised, and claim any support I qualify for during the search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Two years is not enough for me to trust a whole new trade, and the pay could stop before I find another desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could family cover your rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My family would listen, but I would not budget on them paying my rent. I would cancel my planned furniture purchase now and keep the cash where I can reach it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retrain into another role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not want to dress this up as a career opportunity. A qualification might matter for a different regulated role, but I would check entry rules and actual paid posts before signing up.

say: I'd tell colleagues **2028** reaches our thinking work before robots arrive.
I'd ask for written **redundancy terms** while we still have wages.
think: I expect to lose **my own post** if the insurer replaces policy reasoning.
I cannot count on **family money** to cover rent.
do: Request **written redundancy terms** while my current wages continue.
Cancel the planned **furniture purchase** and keep the cash.
Apply for **advertised paid vacancies** and claim eligible support if my post ends.
feel: **Alarmed**, with broken sleep over expected job loss.
S2.quote: I expect the insurer to cut most of our team, including my own post, if full thinking AI is cheaper.
fieldNote: The **robot delay** brings no meaningful shelter to an office job.
Expected loss of **his own job** is already disturbing his sleep.
He will not assume **family support** or buy training without entry and vacancy checks.

steps.text: Claim support he qualifies for during any post-loss job search
Cancel his planned furniture purchase and retain the cash
Apply for advertised paid policy vacancies after losing his post

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2031 gives us five years to get our affairs in order, though the same thinking tasks eventually go. Robots in 2034 change little on a policy desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might still lose this job, but five years lets me build savings while I am paid and see which regulated roles still have people. I will not say a licence guarantees work; a rule can change and a vacancy can disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd ask the insurer what qualifications its compliance staff hold and what a course costs. If there are paid compliance vacancies and I meet the entry rules, I'd enrol after checking the fee; meanwhile I'd add seventy a month to savings. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, if my policy desk is cut, I would ask that local employer about advertised paid paperwork openings, not count on my brother's shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can sleep better than in the two-year version. There is time to check a real path before paying for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your brother have work for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother runs a small shop and might tell me about bookkeeping, but that is not an offered wage. I would visit one local employer and ask what paperwork jobs they actually advertise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your team to retrain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my team about any course rules I find, not pressure them to follow me. They have different bills, and I cannot promise a place to any of them.

say: I'd say **five years** permits saving and checking real qualification rules.
I'd tell my team a **course** is no promise of a post.
think: The insurer may still cut **my position** when AGI handles policy reasoning.
My brother's shop offers **advice**, not a wage I can assume.
do: Check **compliance entry rules** and enrol only if qualified, paid vacancies exist, and the fee makes sense.
Add **seventy monthly** to savings from current pay.
Ask **one local employer** about paid paperwork openings now and after 2031 if displaced.
feel: **Anxious**, though the longer warning eases his sleep.
S3.quote: I will not say a licence guarantees work; a rule can change and a vacancy can disappear.
fieldNote: He insists on **rules and vacancies** before committing to training.
His brother can offer **information**, not dependable income.
He still expects the **thinking work** to change in 2031, ahead of robots.

steps.text: Enrol in compliance course if qualified and paid vacancies justify its fee
Save seventy monthly from his current insurance wages
Ask one local employer about paid paperwork openings now and if displaced after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2036 gives a decade to prepare, if management tells us the truth along the way. The 2039 robots are beside the point for these forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may have moved into a different paid role by 2036, or I may still be here facing a smaller desk. Ten years does not promise a pension or a safe retirement; I would only be 37.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd ask for an annual staffing plan and check local vacancies every three months. I'd keep adding seventy a month to savings and consider a formal compliance course only if its rules and paid openings make sense. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, if my paid hours fall, I would apply only to advertised local paperwork jobs and keep working here until I have another offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I would rather have facts each year than a grand promise about a decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the annual staffing plan tell you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am not going to buy a machine or start a business because an insurer may change its desk. I can do careful paperwork, and I can look for another employer that still pays for that judgment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should new clerks learn meanwhile?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would also make sure new clerks practise difficult renewals instead of only watching software summaries. If a future employer wants human review, they need proof someone can do it.

say: I'd ask management for an **annual staffing plan** with honest dates.
I'd keep new clerks practising **difficult renewals**.
think: I have ten years, but no **promised pension** or secure desk.
I need evidence of **paid openings** before funding a course.
do: Check **local vacancies** quarterly and apply for advertised paid jobs if hours fall after 2036.
Request an **annual staffing plan** while weighing any future course.
feel: **Uneasy**, wanting facts rather than distant promises.
S4.quote: Ten years does not promise a pension or a safe retirement; I would only be 37.
fieldNote: At **27**, he sees 2036 as a midcareer problem, not retirement.
His **resistance to AI** remains, though he would learn required tools with evidence.
He wants **annual staffing facts** and real paid options before paying for a course.

steps.text: Check local vacancies quarterly and apply if hours fall after 2036
Save seventy monthly from his current insurance wages

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect my own desk to go and have too little time to build a bigger cushion. Honest redundancy terms, a paid vacancy list and temporary support I actually qualify for would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to the customer whose renewal is wrong. My name is on the corrections now; someone must still answer for a bad exclusion. Saving wages matters, but so does knowing who takes the call.

headlineQuote: My name is on the corrections now; someone must still answer for a bad exclusion.
portrait: Nikhil is a **27-year-old policy desk lead** with a bachelor's degree and a habit of checking difficult renewals by hand.
He has **modest savings**, typical insurance pay and only some similar employers nearby.
He has **never used AI**, preferring named human responsibility and proof before learning a required tool.
An open vacancy makes the plateau **uneasy**; realistic hour cuts make steady change anxious.
Expected job loss in **2028** wakes him at night; longer timelines allow saving and checking actual paid roles.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his own policy desk before he can build a larger cushion.
whatWouldHelp: Honest **redundancy terms** and a list of real paid vacancies would help.
Temporary **support he qualifies for** could cover part of a job gap.
